title: Visit the sick
hook: I was sick and you visited me
tomorrow: why doesn't the king ask what the prisoner did?

segments.voice: Yesterday, shelter the homeless: no innkeeper in Luke, just no room. The line was make room. Today the room is down a hospital hall.

Fourth floor. The elevator opens on that smell, hand sanitizer and cafeteria gravy. Room 412: the TV on mute, a pudding cup nobody opened, a balloon already sagging. In the bed is someone you love, smaller than you remember. And there you are in the doorway with empty hands. No flowers. No wise words. Nothing that fixes anything. It's tempting to say something useful fast, or to leave. So what is a person in that doorway actually for?
screen: `ROOM 412, THE TV ON MUTE.` → `EMPTY HANDS IN THE DOORWAY.` → `WHAT ARE YOU FOR?`

segments.voice: Jesus answers it in a story about the end of time. A king sorts the nations like a shepherd sorting sheep from goats, and tells the blessed why they're welcome. One reason, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "sick, and you visited me." Look at the verb. Not healed. Not cured. Visited. The just in the story brought no miracle. They came through the door. And they're surprised: when did we see you sick? The king says what they did for the least of his brethren, they did for him. Now a detail worth repeating tonight. In Luke's Gospel, old Zachary holds his newborn son and blesses God because "he hath visited" his people. In Greek, that's the same verb as the king's. The word for God coming close is the word for a chair pulled up to a bed. The Church kept the two together. The Catechism names visiting the sick among the corporal works of mercy, the mercies for the body. The book of Sirach, in Catholic Bibles, says not to be slow to visit the sick. And the letter of James tells the sick to call in the priests to pray over them and anoint them with oil; Catholics see in it the anointing of the sick. A visit needs no training at all. A card, a call, half an hour in a plastic chair. In the doorway, the job is to come in.
screen: `NOT HEALED. VISITED.` · `WHEN DID WE SEE YOU SICK?` · `GOD VISITS; SO DO WE.` · `A CARD, A CALL, A CHAIR.` · then, large: `YOU VISITED ME.`

segments.voice: This one uses your phone. Bring to mind someone who is sick, healing, or stuck at home, and send them a short message that asks nothing back: no question to answer, no advice. If you pray, you can pray for them by name as it sends; if not, let them be the one you hold in mind for the rest of the sit.
Visit the sick. A work of mercy that's mostly showing up: a door, a chair, some time.
Keep this one close: you visited me, not you healed me or you fixed me. Take care.

howItsDone: Catholic priests anoint the seriously ill, lay ministers bring Communion to people at home and in hospitals, and some parishes organize volunteers to visit the homebound.

fork.setup: a teammate's mom is home after surgery. you have ten minutes after practice and nothing clever to say. what fits the king's words best?
options: stop by for ten minutes, sit with her, and ask nothing hard.
read up on her surgery first so you can give real advice.
wait until she's fully better so you don't bother her.
fork.reveal: the king praises the visit, not the cure or the advice, and Sirach says not to be slow about it. a short visit still counts.

original.note: Greek: you visited. the king's word in Matthew 25:36, and Luke's verb for God visiting his people.

chat.says: Abuela fell at the tamale sale. broken wrist, staying overnight. i hate hospitals. does me going even help?
options: Go. The king says you visited me, not you healed me. Showing up is the help.
Only if you can cheer her up. A gloomy visit just makes her feel worse.
Text instead. In a hospital, visiting is really the priest's job anyway.
chat.meaning: In Matthew 25 the verb is visited, not healed or fixed. The work of mercy is coming through the door.

Zachary.meaning: John the Baptist's father, who sings a blessing in Luke 1

Sirach.meaning: a book of wisdom sayings in Catholic Bibles

corporal works of mercy.meaning: the Church's list of mercies for the body

anointing of the sick.meaning: the sacrament of prayer and holy oil for the seriously ill

Catechism.meaning: the Church's official summary of what it teaches

sources.ref: CCC 2447 (works of mercy); CCC 1510–1514 (anointing of the sick)

notes: Douay-Rheims Matthew 25:36 ('sick, and you visited me') and Luke 1:68 ('he hath visited') quoted from memory; confirm.
Greek: Matthew 25:36 ἐπεσκέψασθε and Luke 1:68 ἐπεσκέψατο are both forms of ἐπισκέπτομαι; the voice says 'the same verb'. Confirm.
Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 7:39 Douay, paraphrased as 'not to be slow to visit the sick'; confirm verse numbering.
James 5:14–15 as the scriptural root of the anointing of the sick follows CCC 1510; myth item on anointing 'not only for those at the point of death' follows CCC 1514. Confirm wording.
The hospital room in the hook is an illustration; room number invented.
